title: CR-22: HLD
tldr: Status: in review · Revision: 3 · PRD: approved (revision 5)

items.title: Introduction
items.body:
Status: in review · Revision: 3 · PRD: approved (revision 5)

This document covers components and how they interact. The code-level design goes in the LLD.

items.title: Context
items.body:
Today each `hoop mcp` session tries to serve the pages on the usual address, and the first one wins. When it ends, the pages stop. Reviews already live in one store on the machine, so any server can show every review. Only the tracker and the repository name come from the serving process.

This change moves the pages into one background process that no session owns. Sessions start it when nothing answers, and it outlives them. It restarts itself when its code is out of date, and it stops when nothing has used it for an hour. Short commands such as `hoop submit` start it too when they give a link, but they never register.

```mermaid flowchart LR   B[Browser pages] -->|HTTP on localhost| P[Background pages process]   P --> R[(Review store)]   P --> G[(Session registry)]   M[hoop mcp sessions] -->|register| G   M -->|start when nothing answers| P   C[Commands that give a link] -->|start when nothing answers| P   P -->|reads| T[(Each repository's tracker)]   P -->|compares| V[(hoop's code on disk)]   P -->|restarts into| N[Current hoop install] ```

items.title: Components
items.body:
The registry sits next to the review store. The others are parts of the project HLD's web server and core components.

| Component | Responsibility | Talks to (how) |
|---|---|---|
| Starter (new) | Before it gives a link, a session or command asks the address what it is, waiting at most a second. It uses a hoop server for the same store, and starts the pages process when nothing answers. Anything else leads to the results notice. | HTTP on localhost, and the operating system to start a process. |
| Pages process (new) | It serves the pages on the usual address, apart from every session. It stops after an hour with no live session and no open page. An open page tells the server it is still open. | The operating system, the store and the registry. |
| Registry (new) | It lists each live `hoop mcp` session with its repository, its hoop release and its install. It has a format version, and readers skip what they don't know. | Files in the store's folder, which only the user's own programs can write. |
| Versions (new) | It names the code the pages process started with, and the current code. Current code is the newest release a live session uses, even when it is older than the server's. With no live session, it is the server's own install. | Files on disk and the registry. |
| Self restart (new) | When the pages process is out of date, it starts a successor from the current install and lets go of the address. When its own install is gone and no live session runs, it exits. If the successor doesn't answer in a few seconds, the old process serves again. It tries once for each change of the current code. | The operating system, the address and the audit log. Only its own timer starts it. |
| Pages server (changed) | It serves the page files it started with, so its pages match its routes. It reports its version, its store, whether it is out of date, and the open repositories. | HTTP on localhost, with today's host and origin checks. |
| Picker (changed) | A review page names its review's repository. The tracker page shows the tracker of a chosen open repository. | It asks the pages server for the open repositories. |
| Page start (changed) | When the page's code fails to load, or the server stops answering, the page says what went wrong and how to bring the pages back. | The browser only. |
| Stale notice (new) | The menu shows the serving version. Every page warns while the server is out of date. | It reads the server's report. |
| Results notice (new) | When no hoop server for this store can serve the address, each result with a link says so. It waits for the requester's approval. | The core's results. |

items.title: A session gives a link
items.body:
```mermaid sequenceDiagram   participant S as Session or command   participant A as Usual address   participant P as Pages process   S->>A: what are you? (at most one second)   alt hoop for the same store     A-->>S: hoop, with its store and version   else nothing answers     S->>P: start in the background     P->>A: bind   else something else     S->>S: add the results notice   end   S-->>S: give the link on the usual address ```

The session's tools never wait on the pages, except for the one second check.

items.title: hoop's code changes
items.body:
```mermaid sequenceDiagram   participant P as Old pages process   participant N as Successor   participant A as Usual address   participant B as Browser   P->>P: own timer finds its code out of date   P->>N: start from the current install   P->>A: let go   N->>A: bind, retrying for a few seconds   P->>A: ask what it is   alt successor answers with the current version     P->>P: exit   else no answer in a few seconds     P->>A: bind again, keep the stale notice, and wait for the next change   end   B->>A: next load gets the current code, on the same address ```

The browser keeps its drafts, because the address doesn't change. Pages servers from before this change can't restart themselves, so the first update needs one restart of the session that serves.

items.title: The pages show another repository
items.body:
1. The tracker page asks the server for the open repositories, and gets each one's name and key.
2. The reviewer picks one. The server finds its folder in the registry and reads its tracker.
3. A review page names the repository recorded with the review, whichever repository started the    server.

items.title: Nothing uses the pages
items.body: After an hour with no live session and no open page, the pages process exits. The next session or link starts it again. A page left open then says the pages stopped, and names the step that brings them back.

items.title: Cross-cutting concerns
items.body:
- Security and trust boundaries: the pages stay on this machine, with today's host and origin   checks. No request can make the pages process stop or restart. Only its own timer does, from the   user's own files. A page names a repository only by its name and a key that hides the folder.   So project NFR-13 still holds. A program on this machine that answers like hoop is trusted, as   the PRD assumes.
- Settings: the pages process takes its store, its address and its audit setting from the process   that started it. A successor takes the same ones. The repository comes with each request, from the   registry, so no session's folder holds for every repository.
- Trust in the registry: an entry names the install a restart may run. Only the user's own programs   can write it, and a session the user's Claude runs already runs code as the user. The audit log   records each install the pages process restarts into.
- Removal and rollback: a rollback makes an older release the newest one that live sessions use,   so the pages process restarts into it. An uninstall removes its install, so the process exits   once no live session runs. CR-28's removal steps say how to stop it sooner.
- Version skew: an old pages process now lives only until its timer sees newer code. Until then   every page shows the warning. Writes during that window use the old code, as they do today.
- Several stores: the server reports a key for its store. A session with another store treats it   as something else, so its results say that the pages aren't available.
- Compatibility between releases: the registry has a format version. A reader skips entries of a   newer format and fields it doesn't know. Nothing already stored changes.
- Observability: the menu shows the serving version, and every page shows when it is out of date.   Starts, restarts and stops are written to the audit log.
- Performance: the current code is worked out at most once per page load, within NFR-3.
- Testing strategy: tests start real hoop processes, each on a free address with its own store.   They cover a start, a reuse, a holder that isn't hoop, another store and a self restart. They   also cover a successor that can't start, the idle stop, and restart attempts by request. Browser   tests cover the picker, the warning and the page start error. An acceptance script runs two   sessions in two repositories and ends them.

items.title: What changes in the project design
items.body:
- Project NFR-1 and the project HLD's context say one process serves MCP and the pages. Now the   pages run in their own background process, which sessions start.
- The server's information request named the served folder's repository. Now it names the server's   version, store and state, and lists the open repositories. Project FR-32's frame names the   document's repository.
- `hoop serve` in a terminal works as today. It serves in the foreground, and says so and exits   when hoop for the same store already answers.

items.title: Alternatives considered
items.body:
- Doing nothing: every second session keeps showing the first repository, the pages stop with the   first session, and each stale server is found by hand.
- A free port for each session: drafts in the browser belong to an address, so moving port loses   them. The PRD reviews ruled it out.
- Every session standing by and handing the address over: each session needs a retry loop. A hand   over that fails needs a fallback too. It still stops the pages with the last session. The   first HLD review found the background process simpler.
- Serving page files fresh from disk: an old server would send new pages that call routes it lacks.

items.title: Decisions
items.body:
- D-1 (2026-10-19): The pages run in one background process that no session owns. Context: drafts,   links and the guide depend on one address, and reviews outlive sessions. Consequences: sessions   only start it, and the restart logic lives in one place.
- D-2 (2026-10-19): Only the pages process's own timer can stop or restart it. Context: a web page   can send plain requests to the address. Consequences: no route is added to defend.
- D-3 (2026-10-19): A server serves the page files it started with. Context: a server's pages must   match its routes. Consequences: new page files appear after a restart, not before.
- D-4 (2026-10-19): Out of date means the server's release differs from the newest one a live   session uses, or its own files changed. Context: installs can live in separate folders, rollbacks   happen, and two current checkouts must not switch back and forth. Consequences: two installs of   one release don't restart each other.

items.title: Risks
items.body:
- A crashed session leaves its registry entry. An entry counts only while its process still runs,   so a dead one never picks the install to restart into.
- Two sessions start the pages process at the same moment. The operating system lets only one bind,   and the other exits.
- The code on disk is read while an update is half written. The successor may fail to start, so   the old process serves again and retries on a later check.
